opus-5.5.text:
I think the most exciting problems in formal mathematics sit right at the intersection of those three fields, and none of them alone is enough.

Take the mathematicians first. If you want an AI system that can actually prove theorems, really reason the way a research mathematician does, you need people who understand what a good proof looks like, what the important structures are, and where the real difficulty in a problem lies. They also have taste: they can tell whether a problem is interesting or trivial, and whether a generated proof is elegant or just brute force.

Then there are the AI researchers. They know how to train models, scale them, and design reinforcement learning loops. They understand data, architectures, and how to get a model to explore and improve.

The compiler and programming languages people are the piece that's often underestimated. When you work in a formal system like Lean, a proof is essentially a program, and checking it is a lot like type-checking or compiling code. People with a PL background understand the verification infrastructure deeply: how the proof assistant works under the hood, how to make it fast, and how to build tooling so the model gets clean, reliable feedback. That verifier is what gives you a ground-truth reward signal, which is incredibly valuable for training.

What I find magical is what happens when these people sit in the same room. A mathematician says, "this lemma is really the crux." An AI researcher asks, "how do we get the model to discover that on its own?" And the compiler person says, "here's how we can make checking that a hundred times faster so we can run it at scale." Each of them sees a different part of the elephant.

I also think it reflects where the field is going. AI for math isn't just a machine learning problem, a math problem, or a software engineering problem. It's all three at once. If you only hire one type of person, you get blind spots, and in this area those blind spots are exactly where breakthroughs hide.

On a personal level, I've always loved crossing disciplines. I came from mathematics, and I also spent time thinking about neuroscience and law. I've found that the most creative ideas usually come from collisions between fields. So building a company where that collision happens every day felt very natural to me.

r001.rationale: The response links compiler and programming-language expertise to Lean verification, faster checking, and reliable model feedback, but does not connect compiler techniques to generating Lean data with AI.

r002.rationale: It discusses scaling models and proof checking, but does not say that a limited supply of human Lean experts makes AI generation necessary for producing Lean data at scale.

r003.rationale: It describes mathematicians identifying key lemmas and AI discovering them, but does not connect forward and backward conjecturing to how mathematicians reason.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Because the problem we're trying to solve genuinely sits at the intersection of those three fields, and no single one of them can crack it alone.

If you want a model that doesn't just produce plausible-looking mathematics but mathematics that is actually correct, you need formal verification. That means Lean, and Lean is fundamentally a programming language and a proof assistant. Making a model write Lean well, making the tooling fast enough to run millions of proof attempts, building the infrastructure to check and search over proof states efficiently, that is compiler and systems engineering. The people who understand type theory, elaboration, and how a proof checker actually works are compiler people.

Then there is the AI side. Training models to reason, designing the reinforcement learning loop where the verifier is the reward signal, scaling data, scaling inference. That is a different craft entirely, and the people who do it well have spent years building intuition about what makes models learn.

And then mathematics. Mathematicians are the ones who know what a good problem is, what a meaningful theorem looks like, where the frontier actually is. Without them you optimize toward benchmarks that don't matter. A mathematician can look at a proof the model generated and tell you whether it found something interesting or just brute-forced its way through a trivial corner.

What I've found is that the most important breakthroughs come when someone from one background sees a problem from another background and says, wait, that's actually easy in my world. A compiler engineer looks at a training bottleneck and recognizes it as a search problem they've solved before. A mathematician looks at how we're representing proof states and points out a structure the AI team didn't know existed. That cross-pollination only happens if the people are in the same room, speaking each other's language, and respecting each other's expertise. So we hire for depth in one field and real curiosity about the other two.

r001.rationale: The response links compiler and systems engineering to making models write Lean and to checking proofs, but does not connect compiler techniques to generating Lean data with AI.

r002.rationale: It does not mention a limited supply of human Lean experts or explain that this makes AI generation necessary for producing Lean data at scale.

r003.rationale: It describes mathematicians’ role in identifying meaningful problems and theorem structures, but does not connect forward and backward conjecturing in AI to mathematicians’ reasoning.

astra-6.text:
I think those backgrounds complement each other. People coming from AI are comfortable with learning from data and building systems that can handle ambiguity. Compiler people think about how to turn something high-level into something precise and executable, and how to do that reliably and efficiently. Mathematicians bring a habit of asking, “What exactly are we assuming, and how do we know this is true?”

When you bring those perspectives together, you can connect the flexibility of AI with the rigor of formal reasoning. And the value is in the interaction: someone may recognize that a problem another person has been struggling with has a useful formulation in their field. I want people to be able to challenge each other’s assumptions and build a shared understanding of the problem.

r003.rationale: It discusses mathematicians examining assumptions and people challenging each other, but does not connect forward and backward conjecturing in AI to mathematicians’ reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those backgrounds bring complementary ways of thinking. People working in AI are comfortable with learning, experimentation, and systems that are probabilistic. Compiler engineers think carefully about how to turn a high-level idea into something that runs correctly and efficiently. Mathematicians bring precision: What exactly are we claiming, and why should it be true?

When you bring those people together, they can challenge each other’s assumptions. A promising model capability becomes much more useful when you can connect it to rigorous reasoning and reliable execution. That’s why I value the collaboration—the problems we’re trying to solve span all three areas.
